steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on unsupervised domain adaptation for nighttime semantic segmentation, which focuses on dynamic and small objects; cover the background, the shortcomings of existing UDA methods, our framework and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Semantic segmentation and the difficulty of nighttime scenes
- Existing UDA methods for nighttime segmentation and their limits
- Motivation: our one-stage UDA framework (DSR and FPA modules)
- Experimental highlights
- Summary of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - semantic segmentation essential for scene understanding in autonomous driving and robotic systems
  - big progress with deep neural networks (DNNs)
  - but mostly target daytime images; performance drops drastically in challenging environments e.g. nighttime, especially dynamic and small objects
  - other modalities help (thermal cameras, event cameras), but single-modal bottleneck: inadequate illumination + scarce annotated datasets
- UDA methods
  - adapt model trained on source (daytime) to unlabeled target (nighttime)
  - type 1: style transfer models (e.g. CycleGAN) generate daytime/nighttime images as intermediate domain; cumbersome multi-stage learning; fails if style transfer fails
  - type 2: twilight images with coarsely aligned day-night pairs in target domain; progressive adaptation day -> night
  - type 3: prior GPS knowledge or static loss to reduce influence of coarse alignment; better pseudo labels
  - all pay less attention to dynamic and small objects (vehicles, poles); hard to transfer because of misalignment (Fig. 1)
  - patch-wise / pixel-wise contrastive learning UDA: hard to get semantic contexts in under-exposed conditions
- Our framework (Motivation)
  - one-stage UDA framework, attention to dynamic and small objects
  - DSR (dynamic and small objects refinement) module: composite mask from source ground truth, emphasizes dynamic and small objects + randomly selected classes; memory bank stores long-tailed objects across images (Sec. III-B)
  - mixup creates a new mixed domain with domain shift vs source daytime and target nighttime
  - FPA (feature prototype alignment) module: aligns source with mixed and target nighttime domains (Sec. III-C); prototypes from source labels and mixed-domain pseudo-labels; contrastive loss pulls same-class features from other domain closer, pushes negatives away; same for source and target nighttime
  - adaptive re-weighting mechanism in FPA for dynamic and small categories
- Experiments
  - Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, ACDC; beat SoTA in most categories, esp. dynamic and small objects
  - mIoU: pole 60.9%, car 86.8%, bus 25.2%; +2.9%, +3.0%, +20.2% absolute over SoTA
- Contributions (three-fold)
  - (I) problem: dynamic and small objects + domain shifts from illumination and style
  - (II) UDA framework with DSR and FPA modules
  - (III) experiments on Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, ACDC-night: new SoTA

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is essential for scene understanding in autonomous driving and robotic systems. Recently semantic segmentation made remarkable progress with the development of deep neural networks (DNNs). But existing methods mostly target daytime images. So their performance drops a lot in challenging environments, e.g., nighttime, and especially for dynamic and small objects. Many approaches use other modalities to help nighttime segmentation, i.e., thermal cameras and event cameras, but for single-modal semantic segmentation at night the bottleneck is the lower performance that comes from inadequate illumination and the scarcity of annotated datasets.

To deal with this problem, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods were developed to adapt the model, which is trained with source domain (i.e., daytime) images, to learn from unlabeled target domain (i.e., nighttime) images. The main methods fall into three types: 1) Some methods use style transfer models, e.g., CycleGAN, to generate daytime or nighttime images, and these images serve as an intermediate domain connecting the source and target domains. But these methods are cumbersome because they need multi-stage learning, and the performance is not guaranteed if the style transfer fails. 2) Other methods use twilight images with the coarsely aligned day-night image pairs in the target domain to adapt progressively from the daytime to the nighttime domain. 3) The rest of the methods use prior GPS knowledge or a static loss to reduce the influence of coarsely aligned day-night image pairs, which makes the pseudo labels better. However, these methods pay less attention to dynamic and small objects in nighttime images, e.g., vehicles and poles, and these are especially hard to transfer from the daytime domain to the nighttime domain because of their misalignment, as shown in Fig. 1. Also, existing UDA methods with patch-wise or pixel-wise contrastive learning have trouble getting effective semantic contexts within patches or pixels when the images are under-exposed.

Motivation:
- one-stage UDA framework, more attention to dynamic and small objects; two modules: DSR and FPA
- DSR: composite mask from source ground truth (dynamic and small objects + randomly selected classes); memory bank for long-tailed objects (Sec. III-B)
- mixup forms a mixed domain -> FPA aligns source with mixed and target nighttime domains (Sec. III-C); prototypes + contrastive loss; adaptive re-weighting
- experiments: Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, ACDC; pole 60.9%, car 86.8%, bus 25.2% mIoU (+2.9%, +3.0%, +20.2%)
- contributions (I) problem, (II) framework with DSR and FPA, (III) new SoTA on Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, ACDC-night

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is essential for scene understanding in autonomous driving and robotic systems. Recently semantic segmentation made remarkable progress with the development of deep neural networks (DNNs). But existing methods mostly target daytime images. So their performance drops a lot in challenging environments, e.g., nighttime, and especially for dynamic and small objects. Many approaches use other modalities to help nighttime segmentation, i.e., thermal cameras and event cameras, but for single-modal semantic segmentation at night the bottleneck is the lower performance that comes from inadequate illumination and the scarcity of annotated datasets.

To deal with this problem, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods were developed to adapt the model, which is trained with source domain (i.e., daytime) images, to learn from unlabeled target domain (i.e., nighttime) images. The main methods fall into three types: 1) Some methods use style transfer models, e.g., CycleGAN, to generate daytime or nighttime images, and these images serve as an intermediate domain connecting the source and target domains. But these methods are cumbersome because they need multi-stage learning, and the performance is not guaranteed if the style transfer fails. 2) Other methods use twilight images with the coarsely aligned day-night image pairs in the target domain to adapt progressively from the daytime to the nighttime domain. 3) The rest of the methods use prior GPS knowledge or a static loss to reduce the influence of coarsely aligned day-night image pairs, which makes the pseudo labels better. However, these methods pay less attention to dynamic and small objects in nighttime images, e.g., vehicles and poles, and these are especially hard to transfer from the daytime domain to the nighttime domain because of their misalignment, as shown in Fig. 1. Also, existing UDA methods with patch-wise or pixel-wise contrastive learning have trouble getting effective semantic contexts within patches or pixels when the images are under-exposed.

Motivation: In this paper we propose a new one-stage UDA framework for nighttime semantic segmentation that pays more attention to dynamic and small objects. Our framework has two key technical modules: the dynamic and small objects refinement (DSR) module and the feature prototype alignment (FPA) module. First, the DSR module generates a composite mask from the ground truth of the source domain, which emphasizes dynamic and small objects and also randomly selected classes. We also introduce a memory bank that stores the long-tailed objects across images, which complements these low-occurring categories from different images (Sec. III-B). We observe that the mixup operation forms a new domain, the mixed domain, which has a domain shift with the source daytime domain and the target nighttime domain. So we propose the FPA module to align the source domain with both the mixed domain and the target nighttime domain, to reduce the domain gap in general (Sec. III-C). FPA extracts reliable prototypes from the labels in the source domain and the pseudo-labels in the mixed domain, and with a contrastive loss it pulls features of the same classes from the other domain closer as positive pairs and pushes other negative pairs away. The same operation is done for the source and target nighttime domain. We also design an adaptive re-weighting mechanism in the FPA module to improve the attention on some dynamic and small categories. Extensive experiments on the Dark Zurich, the Nighttime Driving, and ACDC datasets outperform the state-of-the-art (SoTA) in most categories, especially for identifying dynamic and small objects. Our approach got mean intersection over union (mIoU) scores of 60.9% for the ’pole’ category, 86.8% for the ’car’ category, and 25.2% for the ’bus’ category, which is an improvement of 2.9%, 3.0% and 20.2% absolute performance over the SoTA method, respectively.

To sum up, the main contributions of this work are three: (I) We study the crucial problem of improving the performance of dynamic and small objects and reducing the domain shifts that come from illumination and style differences. (II) We propose a new UDA framework for nighttime semantic segmentation with the dynamic and small objects refinement (DSR) module and the feature prototype alignment (FPA) module. (III) Extensive experiments on the Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, and ACDC-night datasets show that our method gets a new SoTA performance for nighttime semantic segmentation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is essential for scene understanding of autonomous driving [1,2,3,4,5,6] and robotic systems [7,8,9,10]. Recently, with the development of deep neural networks (DNNs), semantic segmentation has achieved remarkable progress. However, existing methods mainly target daytime images [11,12,13]. Thus their performance drops drastically in challenging environments, e.g., nighttime [14,15,16], especially for dynamic and small objects. Many approaches leverage other modalities to assist nighttime segmentation, i.e., thermal cameras [17,18] and event cameras [19,20], but the bottleneck of single-modal semantic segmentation at nighttime lies in the decreased performance resulting from inadequate illumination and the scarcity of annotated datasets.

To tackle the problem, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods have been developed to adapt the model trained with source domain (i.e., daytime) images to learn from unlabeled target domain (i.e., nighttime) images. The prevailing methods can be categorized into three types: 1) Some methods, e.g., [21,22,14,23,15,24], use style transfer models, e.g., CycleGAN [25], to generate daytime or nighttime images, which serve as an intermediate domain connecting the source and target domains. However, these methods are cumbersome as they require multi-stage learning, and the performance cannot be guaranteed if style transfer fails. 2) Other methods use twilight images with the coarsely aligned day-night image pairs in the target domain to progressively adapt from the daytime to the nighttime domain [26,14,15]. 3) The remaining methods leverage prior GPS knowledge or a static loss to reduce the influence of coarsely aligned day-night image pairs, which improves the quality of pseudo labels [16,27,28,29,30]. However, they pay less attention to the dynamic and small objects, e.g., vehicles and poles, in nighttime images, which are particularly challenging to transfer from the daytime domain to the nighttime domain due to their misalignment, as shown in Fig. 1. Also, existing UDA methods employing patch-wise or pixel-wise contrastive learning [31,32] struggle to acquire effective semantic contexts within patches or pixels in under-exposed conditions.

Motivation: In this paper, we propose a novel one-stage UDA framework for nighttime semantic segmentation that pays more attention to dynamic and small objects. Specifically, our framework consists of two key technical modules: the dynamic and small objects refinement (DSR) module and the feature prototype alignment (FPA) module. Firstly, the DSR module generates a composite mask from the ground truth of the source domain, emphasizing dynamic and small objects as well as randomly selected classes. We also introduce a memory bank to store the long-tailed objects across images, which complements these low-occurring categories from different images (Sec. III-B). We observe that the mixup operation forms a new domain—the mixed domain—that has a domain shift with the source daytime and target nighttime domains. Therefore, we propose the FPA module to align the source domain with both the mixed and the target nighttime domain, aiming to reduce the domain gap in general (Sec. III-C). FPA extracts reliable prototypes from labels in the source domain and pseudo-labels in the mixed domain, pulling the features with the same classes from the other domain closer as positive pairs and pushing other negative pairs away via a contrastive loss. Note that the same operation is conducted for the source and target nighttime domains. We further design an adaptive re-weighting mechanism to improve the attention to some dynamic and small categories in the FPA module. Extensive experiments on the Dark Zurich [14], the Nighttime Driving [26], and ACDC [33] datasets outperform the state-of-the-art (SoTA) in most categories, particularly in identifying dynamic and small objects. Notably, our approach achieves mean intersection over union (mIoU) scores of 60.9% for the ’pole’ category, 86.8% for the ’car’ category, and 25.2% for the ’bus’ category, a significant improvement of 2.9%, 3.0% and 20.2% absolute performance, respectively, over the SoTA method.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are three-fold: (I) We study the crucial problem of focusing more on improving the performance of dynamic and small objects and reducing the domain shifts caused by illumination and style differences. (II) We propose a novel UDA framework for nighttime semantic segmentation by designing the dynamic and small objects refinement (DSR) module and the feature prototype alignment (FPA) module. (III) Extensive experiments on the Dark Zurich, Nighttime Driving, and ACDC-night datasets verify that our method achieves a new SoTA performance for nighttime semantic segmentation.

References:
